questions.question_text: Differentiate $y = 9e^{7x}$. Give your answer in simplest form.

options.why: Treated $e^{7x}$ as its own derivative; only $e^{x}$ has that property.
Multiplied by the index coefficient $7$ but dropped the coefficient $9$.
Reduced the index by $1$, as if the power rule applied to an exponential.

questions.question_text: Differentiate $y = 10e^{-\frac{x}{5}}$. Give your answer in simplest form.

options.why: Multiplied by the index coefficient but dropped the coefficient $10$.
Lost the negative sign carried by the index coefficient $-\dfrac{1}{5}$.
Multiplied by $-5$, the reciprocal of the index coefficient, instead of by $-\dfrac{1}{5}$.

questions.question_text: Differentiate $y = e^{8-3x}$. Give your answer in simplest form.

options.why: Left out the multiplier $-3$ from the index.
Used the constant term $8$ as the multiplier instead of the coefficient of $x$.
Differentiated the index as well, replacing $8-3x$ with $-3x$; the index must stay unchanged.

questions.question_text: Differentiate $f(x) = 2e^{5x} - 3e^{-4x}$. Give your answer in simplest form.

options.why: Kept the original minus sign, missing that $-3 \times -4 = +12$.
Treated each $e^{ax}$ as its own derivative, so no index multiplier was applied.
Replaced each coefficient with the index coefficient instead of multiplying the two together.

questions.question_text: Differentiate $y = \sqrt{e^{6x}}$. Give your answer in simplest form.

options.why: Differentiated $e^{6x}$ and ignored the square root altogether.
Halved the index in the multiplier but left the index in the exponent unhalved.
Used the $\dfrac{1}{2}$ from the square root as the multiplier instead of the new index $3$.

questions.question_text: For $y = e^{4x+1}$, find the exact value of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ at $x = -\dfrac{1}{4}$.

options.why: Evaluated the function value $y = e^{0} = 1$ instead of the derivative.
Substituted $x = 0$ rather than $x = -\dfrac{1}{4}$ into the derivative.

questions.question_text: The curve $y = e^{ax+2}$ has gradient $-6e^{2}$ at $x = 0$. Find $a$.

options.why: Dropped the negative sign when comparing $ae^{2}$ with $-6e^{2}$.
Read the whole gradient as the value of $a$ without dividing by $e^{2}$.
Used the coefficient $3$ as the multiplier instead of the index coefficient $-7$.
Lost the negative sign from the index coefficient $-7$.
Assumed every exponential is its own derivative, which is true only for $e^{x}$.

questions.question_text: To differentiate $y = e^{9x-4}$ by the chain rule, let $u = 9x - 4$. Which line correctly completes $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{dy}{du} \times \dfrac{du}{dx}$?

options.why: Multiplied by $u$ itself instead of by $\dfrac{du}{dx} = 9$.
Took $\dfrac{du}{dx} = 1$, ignoring the coefficient of $x$ in the index.
Applied the factor $9$ twice, once to $\dfrac{dy}{du}$ and once to $\dfrac{du}{dx}$.

questions.solution_text:
Let $u = 9x - 4$, so $\dfrac{du}{dx} = 9$.
Let $y = e^{u}$, so $\dfrac{dy}{du} = e^{u}$.
$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = e^{u} \times 9$
$= 9e^{9x-4}$
